topic: Commercial performance and ground reference manoeuvres

notes.front: What is a steep spiral?
notes.back: A gliding turn flown at constant radius around a point on the ground, to lose a lot of altitude quickly over that spot.
notes.explanation: The manoeuvre combines a glide with ground-track control, so the airplane comes down without drifting away from the chosen spot.
notes.example: Like turns around a point, but with the throttle closed, so each circle is flown lower than the one before.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: The objective of the steep spiral is to provide a flight maneuver for rapidly dissipating substantial amounts of altitude while remaining over a selected spot.

notes.front: What is a chandelle?
notes.back: A maximum-performance 180° climbing turn from about straight-and-level flight, ending wings level and nose high just above stall speed.
notes.explanation: It asks for the most climb the chosen bank and power can give, finishing at the slowest controllable speed.
notes.example: Like reversing direction over a valley by climbing out of it in one smooth half-circle, trading speed for height.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: A chandelle is a maximum performance, 180° climbing turn that begins from approximately straight-and-level flight and concludes with the airplane in a wings-level, nose-high attitude just above stall speed.

notes.front: What is a lazy eight?
notes.back: Two opposing 180° turns, each climbing for its first 90° and descending for its second 90°.
notes.explanation: Pitch, bank and airspeed change all the way through, so it trains coordination across a wide range of speeds and attitudes.
notes.example: Like S-turns across a road, but with each half-circle rising and then falling, so the nose traces an eight lying on its side.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: The lazy eight adds both a climb and descent to each 180° segment. The first 90° is a climb; the second 90° is a descent.

notes.front: What are eights on pylons?
notes.back: A figure eight around two ground points, varying altitude so a sight line parallel to the lateral axis stays on each pylon.
notes.explanation: The pilot holds a visual reference on the pylon rather than a fixed ground track, which the handbook calls unmatched for intuitive control.
notes.example: Like circling two silos in turn, keeping each silo pinned to the same spot beside you on the window frame.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: The goal of eights on pylons is to keep the line from the pilot's eyes to the pylon parallel to the lateral axis.

notes.front: What is the pivotal altitude?
notes.back: The altitude at which, for a given groundspeed, the line of sight to the pylon appears to pivot on it.
notes.explanation: At that altitude the reference line neither moves forward nor back across the ground, so the pylon stays put.
notes.example: Like finding the one height on a carousel horse at which a lamppost outside seems to stay fixed beside your shoulder.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: The pivotal altitude is the altitude at which, for a given groundspeed, the projection of the visual reference line to the pylon appears to pivot.

notes.front: What is a power-off accuracy approach?
notes.back: Gliding with the engine idling, in a set pattern, to touch down at a given point or within a set distance beyond it.
notes.explanation: It builds the judgement and procedures to fly the airplane accurately to a safe landing without power.
notes.example: Like rolling a ball to stop on a mark with one push: all the planning happens before you let go.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "Power-Off Accuracy Approaches"
notes.evidence: Power-off accuracy approaches and landings involve gliding to a touchdown at a given point (or within a specified distance beyond that point), while using a specific pattern and with the engine idling.

notes.front: What is a 180-degree power-off approach?
notes.back: A glide at idle power from a point on the downwind leg to a preselected landing spot.
notes.explanation: It extends the 90° power-off approach: the glide starts higher and includes a turn to reach the base-leg position at the right height.
notes.example: Like a simulated engine failure beside the runway, but at a chosen point, aiming for a chosen spot.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "180° Power-Off Approach"
notes.evidence: The 180° power-off approach is executed by gliding with idle power from a given point on a downwind leg to a preselected landing spot.

notes.front: On the commercial practical test, the applicant rolls into a coordinated 360° steep turn with approximately a {{c1::50°}} bank.
notes.explanation: The commercial target is steeper than the private test's approximately 45°.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task A "Steep Turns", CA.V.A.S3
notes.evidence: Roll into a coordinated 360° steep turn with approximately a 50° bank.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In the commercial steep turn, what altitude and airspeed tolerances apply?
notes.back: Entry altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots.
notes.explanation: Both are held against the entry values while the bank is kept steady and the turn is completed.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task A "Steep Turns", CA.V.A.S5
notes.evidence: Maintain the entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, and roll out on the entry heading ±10°.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a commercial checkride you hold 42° of bank throughout the steep turn. Is the bank within the standard?
notes.back: No: the target is about 50° ±5°, so at least 45°.
notes.explanation: The bank tolerance is measured around the commercial target of approximately 50°, not the private 45°.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it is within ±10° of 50°
B) No, it is below 50° ±5°
C) Yes, any bank of 30° or more is steep
D) Yes, it is within ±5° of 45°
notes.choicesExplained: A uses the heading tolerance, not the bank tolerance. C confuses steep turns with medium banks. D applies the private-pilot target, not the commercial one.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task A "Steep Turns", CA.V.A.S3 and S5
notes.evidence: Roll into a coordinated 360° steep turn with approximately a 50° bank.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: If the manufacturer gives no recommended steep-turn airspeed, what limits the entry speed on the commercial test?
notes.back: An airspeed not above maneuvering speed (VA).
notes.explanation: The manufacturer's figure comes first; only without one does VA become the ceiling.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task A "Steep Turns", CA.V.A.S2
notes.evidence: Establish the manufacturer's recommended airspeed; or if one is not available, an airspeed not to exceed maneuvering speed (VA).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Your pilot's operating handbook gives no steep-turn speed. At today's weight VA is 98 knots and cruise is 115 knots. What entry speed do you pick?
notes.back: A speed no higher than 98 knots (VA).
notes.explanation: Without a manufacturer figure, the standard caps the entry speed at maneuvering speed, whatever the cruise speed.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task A "Steep Turns", CA.V.A.S2
notes.evidence: Establish the manufacturer's recommended airspeed; or if one is not available, an airspeed not to exceed maneuvering speed (VA).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What range of bank does the Airplane Flying Handbook give for steep turns?
notes.back: Between 45° and 60°.
notes.explanation: The handbook range covers both the private and commercial test targets and turns of 360° or 720°.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Turns"
notes.evidence: Steep turns consist of single to multiple 360° and 720° turns, in either or both directions, using a bank angle between 45° and 60°.

notes.front: In what real situation may the steep spiral be useful?
notes.back: During an emergency landing.
notes.explanation: Losing height while staying over a chosen spot lets a pilot descend above a landing area before the approach.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: This maneuver may be useful during an emergency landing.

notes.front: At 6,000 feet above the ground your engine fails directly above a long, empty field. Which training manoeuvre lets you lose height while staying over it?
notes.back: A steep spiral.
notes.explanation: The steep spiral is the manoeuvre designed to shed a lot of altitude while remaining over a selected spot.
notes.choices:
A) A chandelle
B) A lazy eight
C) A steep spiral
D) Eights on pylons
notes.choicesExplained: A is a maximum-performance climbing turn. B alternates climbs and descents at roughly constant altitude overall. D is flown at the pivotal altitude, not a descent.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: The objective of the steep spiral is to provide a flight maneuver for rapidly dissipating substantial amounts of altitude while remaining over a selected spot.

notes.front: A steep spiral consists of at least {{c1::three}} 360° turns.
notes.explanation: Several full turns make the pilot correct for wind on every heading while keeping a constant radius.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: The maneuver consists of the completion of at least three 360° turns

notes.front: A steep spiral should begin high enough that it ends no lower than {{c1::1,500 feet}} above ground level.
notes.explanation: The entry height must allow for all the turns and still leave this margin at the end.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: should begin at sufficient altitude such that the maneuver concludes no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL).

notes.front: The ground below is at 1,000 feet above sea level. You expect to lose about 600 feet per turn in a three-turn steep spiral. What is the lowest height above sea level to start?
notes.back: About 4,300 feet: 2,500 feet (1,500 above ground) plus 1,800 feet for three turns.
notes.explanation: The spiral must finish at least 1,500 feet above the ground, so the loss for all three turns is added on top of that floor.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: should begin at sufficient altitude such that the maneuver concludes no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the steepest bank allowed in a steep spiral?
notes.back: 60°, at the steepest point of the turn.
notes.explanation: The distance from the reference point sets the radius, and the bank must stay within this limit where wind makes it steepest.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: The pilot should consider the distance from the reference point since that establishes the turning radius, and the steepest bank should not exceed 60°.

notes.front: How does the pilot correct for wind to keep a constant radius in a steep spiral?
notes.back: Steepen the bank on downwind headings and shallow it on upwind headings.
notes.explanation: The pilot keeps correcting for changes in wind direction and velocity to hold a constant radius.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: This can only be accomplished by proper correction for wind drift by steepening the bank on downwind headings and shallowing the bank on upwind headings.

notes.front: In a steep spiral you are turning onto a downwind heading and already have 55° of bank. The circle is drifting wider. What do you do?
notes.back: Steepen the bank, but no further than 60°.
notes.explanation: Downwind headings need the steepest bank to hold the radius, and the spiral limit is 60°, so there is only 5° to spare.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: The pilot should consider the distance from the reference point since that establishes the turning radius, and the steepest bank should not exceed 60°.

notes.front: Why should the throttle be advanced for a few seconds from time to time during a steep spiral?
notes.back: Long idling in the glide may cause excessive engine cooling, spark plug fouling or carburettor ice.
notes.explanation: Briefly advancing the throttle helps avoid these problems; cylinder head temperature gauges, if fitted, show the cooling.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: Operating the engine at idle speed for any prolonged period during the glide may result in excessive engine cooling, spark plug fouling, or carburetor ice. To assist in avoiding these issues, the throttle should be periodically advanced and sustained for a few seconds.

notes.front: How does a steep spiral differ from an emergency descent?
notes.back: The reasons for flying them may differ, and the airspeed and configuration are usually different.
notes.explanation: Both lose altitude quickly, but only the spiral is flown around a ground reference as a gliding turn.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Steep Spiral"
notes.evidence: Note that while there are similarities between a steep spiral and an emergency descent, the reasons for using the two maneuvers may differ, and the airspeed and configuration are usually different.

notes.front: Is a chandelle judged on how much altitude is gained?
notes.back: No: on the proficiency shown in getting the most climb from the chosen bank and power.
notes.explanation: The aim is maximum climb, but the standard is the skill shown, not a number of feet.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: the standard used to judge the maneuver is not the amount of altitude gained, but rather the pilot’s proficiency as it pertains to maximizing climb performance for the power and bank selected

notes.front: The first 90° of a chandelle is flown with {{c1::constant bank and continuously increasing pitch}}.
notes.explanation: Pitch rises at a rate that reaches its maximum just as the turn passes 90°.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: The first 90° of turn is described as constant bank and continuously increasing pitch; and the second 90° as constant pitch and continuously decreasing bank.

notes.front: The second 90° of a chandelle is flown with {{c1::constant pitch and continuously decreasing bank}}.
notes.explanation: The pitch reached at 90° is held while a slow, constant-rate roll-out brings the wings level at 180°.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: The first 90° of turn is described as constant bank and continuously increasing pitch; and the second 90° as constant pitch and continuously decreasing bank.

notes.front: What bank angle is used in a chandelle?
notes.back: About 30°.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the bank is generally 30°, and the commercial standard asks for approximately 30°.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task C "Chandelles", CA.V.C.S4
notes.evidence: Establish the angle of bank at approximately 30°.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A pilot begins a chandelle with only 15° of bank and pitches up at the usual rate. What is the likely result?
notes.back: A stall before the turn is complete.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists an initial bank that is too shallow, resulting in a stall, among common chandelle errors.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle", common errors
notes.evidence: Initial bank is too shallow resulting in a stall

notes.front: A pilot begins a chandelle with 45° of bank. What does the handbook say this error causes?
notes.back: Failure to gain maximum performance.
notes.explanation: Too steep an initial bank is listed as a common error that costs climb performance.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle", common errors
notes.evidence: Initial bank is too steep resulting in failure to gain maximum performance

notes.front: At what airspeed is a chandelle entered?
notes.back: The manufacturer's recommended speed, which in many cases is the design maneuvering speed (VA).
notes.explanation: The entry is from straight-and-level flight or a shallow dive, and the manufacturer's figure comes first.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: The maneuver should be entered from straight-and-level flight or a shallow dive at an airspeed recommended by the manufacturer—in many cases this is the airplane’s design maneuvering speed (VA)

notes.front: Where should the flaps and any retractable landing gear be before a chandelle?
notes.back: Up.
notes.explanation: The chandelle is a maximum-performance climb, and the task asks for the configuration suited to it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: Prior to starting the chandelle, the flaps and landing gear (if retractable) should be in the UP position.

notes.front: Before a chandelle, a candidate leaves 10° of flap set "for extra lift". What should the examiner expect instead?
notes.back: Flaps (and retractable gear) up before the manoeuvre starts.
notes.explanation: The handbook sets the chandelle up clean, and the task asks for the configuration for a maximum-performance climb.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task C "Chandelles", CA.V.C.K3
notes.evidence: Appropriate airplane configuration for maximum performance climb.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At the 180° point of a chandelle, what should the wings, airspeed and pitch be?
notes.back: Wings level, airspeed just above the power-on stall speed, and the nose-high attitude held momentarily.
notes.explanation: Only after that moment of controlled flight is the pitch lowered back to cruise.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: At the completion of 180° of turn, the wings should be level to the horizon, the airspeed should be just above the power-on stall speed, and the airplane’s pitch-high attitude should be held momentarily.

notes.front: You finish a chandelle wings level at 180°, but the airspeed is well above stall speed. What went wrong?
notes.back: The pitch attitude was too low.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes that if pitch is set too low, the airspeed never decreases to just above stall speed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: If the pitch attitude is set too low, the airplane’s airspeed will never decrease to just above stall speed.

notes.front: How does right rudder pressure change as airspeed decreases in a chandelle?
notes.back: It is progressively increased to stay coordinated.
notes.explanation: As airspeed decreases, left-turning tendencies such as P-factor have more effect.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: As airspeed decreases during the chandelle, left-turning tendencies, such as P-factor, have greater effect. As airspeed decreases, right rudder pressure is progressively increased to ensure that the airplane remains in coordinated flight.

notes.front: Which roll-out needs more right rudder near the end of a chandelle: from a left chandelle or from a right one?
notes.back: From a left chandelle.
notes.explanation: The handbook singles out the roll-out from a left chandelle, where left adverse yaw adds to left-turning tendencies such as P-factor.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: right rudder pressure is significant, especially when rolling out from a left chandelle due to left adverse yaw and left-turning tendencies, such as P-factor.

notes.front: You are flying a chandelle and reach the 90° point with maximum pitch set. What do you do next?
notes.back: Hold that pitch and begin a slow, coordinated, constant-rate roll-out, reaching wings level at 180°.
notes.explanation: The second half keeps pitch constant while the bank decreases.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: Starting at the 90° point, and while maintaining the pitch attitude set at the end of the first 90°, the pilot begins a slow and coordinated constant rate rollout so as to have the wings level when the airplane is at the 180° point.

notes.front: Your airplane's manual recommends 110 knots to enter a chandelle; its VA today is 104 knots. Which entry speed does the handbook point you to?
notes.back: The manufacturer's recommended 110 knots.
notes.explanation: The handbook enters at the manufacturer's speed; VA is only what that speed often turns out to be.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: The maneuver should be entered from straight-and-level flight or a shallow dive at an airspeed recommended by the manufacturer

notes.front: During the roll-out in a chandelle, why is a slight increase in elevator back pressure needed?
notes.back: Speed keeps decreasing, so extra back pressure stops the pitch attitude from decreasing.
notes.explanation: The task asks for pitch control suited to continuously decreasing airspeed while the pitch is held constant.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: However, as speed continues to decrease, a slight increase of elevator back pressure is required to keep the pitch attitude from decreasing.

notes.front: On the commercial test, how low may a chandelle or a lazy eight be flown?
notes.back: No lower than 1,500 feet above ground level.
notes.explanation: Both tasks ask the applicant to select an altitude that keeps the whole manoeuvre above this height.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task C "Chandelles", CA.V.C.S2
notes.evidence: Select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In the figure, which quantity is held constant in each half of the chandelle?
notes.back: First 90°: bank constant. Second 90°: pitch constant.
notes.explanation: In each half one quantity is held while the other changes: pitch rises in the first half, bank falls in the second.

image.alt: A graph of a chandelle against degrees of turn from 0 to 180. The bank line rises quickly to about 30 degrees and stays level until 90 degrees, then falls steadily to zero at 180 degrees. The pitch line rises steadily from level to its maximum at 90 degrees and then stays constant to 180 degrees. A note says airspeed falls throughout and ends just above the power-on stall speed.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10, "Chandelle" (see Figure 10-3)

notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Chandelle"
notes.evidence: A chandelle is best described in two specific phases: the first 90° of turn and the second 90° of turn.

notes.front: What makes the lazy eight unique among standard flight training manoeuvres?
notes.back: It is the only one in which flight control pressures are constantly changing.
notes.explanation: It is designed to develop coordination of the controls across a wide range of airspeeds and attitudes.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: It is the only standard flight training maneuver in which flight control pressures are constantly changing.

notes.front: An instructor wants a manoeuvre in which the pilot never holds a steady control pressure. Which one fits?
notes.back: The lazy eight.
notes.explanation: Chandelles hold bank, then pitch, constant; the lazy eight is the one where control pressures change all the time.
notes.choices:
A) Chandelle
B) Lazy eight
C) Steep turn
D) Steep spiral
notes.choicesExplained: A holds bank constant for 90°, then pitch. C holds a steady bank for the whole turn. D holds a constant glide speed and changes bank only for wind.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: It is the only standard flight training maneuver in which flight control pressures are constantly changing.

notes.front: Where are the reference points for each 180° turn of a lazy eight?
notes.back: At 45°, 90° and 135° from the direction in which the manoeuvre starts.
notes.explanation: The points on the natural horizon help make the climbing and descending turns symmetrical.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: The reference points selected should be at 45°, 90°, and 135° from the direction in which the maneuver is started for each 180° turn.

notes.front: In a lazy eight, what should pitch and bank be at the 45° reference point?
notes.back: Maximum pitch up, with about 15° of bank.
notes.explanation: The climbing turn is planned so the highest pitch arrives at this point while the bank keeps slowly increasing.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: The climbing turn should be planned and controlled so that the maximum pitch-up attitude is reached at the 45° point with an approximate bank angle of 15°.

notes.front: In a lazy eight, what should bank and pitch be at the 90° reference point?
notes.back: Bank at its maximum of about 30°, with the pitch attitude passing through level.
notes.explanation: This is the top of the climb, so pitch is crossing the horizon on its way down.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: At the lazy eight’s 90° reference point, the bank angle should also have reached its maximum angle of approximately 30°.

notes.front: At the 90° point of a lazy eight, airspeed is at its minimum, about {{c1::5 to 10 knots}} above stall speed.
notes.explanation: The climb has used up speed, and the pilot must keep going into the descending turn without hesitating.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: The airspeed should be at its minimum, just about 5 to 10 knots above stall speed, with the airplane’s pitch attitude passing through level flight.

notes.front: In a lazy eight, where in each 180° turn is the pitch attitude lowest?
notes.back: At the 135° point.
notes.explanation: After 90° the bank is reduced slowly while the nose is allowed to fall, reaching its lowest point here.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: When the airplane has turned 135°, the airplane should be in its lowest pitch attitude.

notes.front: In a lazy eight the nose is crossing the horizon, the bank is at its steepest and the airspeed is lowest. Which reference point is this?
notes.back: The 90° point.
notes.explanation: The 90° point is where maximum bank, minimum airspeed and level pitch coincide.
notes.choicesExplained: A is where pitch is highest, with only about 15° of bank. C is where pitch is lowest. D is where wings and nose are level at the entry airspeed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: The airspeed should be at its minimum, just about 5 to 10 knots above stall speed, with the airplane’s pitch attitude passing through level flight.

notes.front: In the descending part of a lazy eight the nose is at its lowest. Which reference point should you be passing?
notes.back: The 135° point.
notes.explanation: The lowest pitch is planned for 135°, after which pitch and bank are brought back to level by 180°.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: When the airplane has turned 135°, the airplane should be in its lowest pitch attitude.

notes.front: Using the figure, what happens at each reference point in one half of a lazy eight?
notes.back: 45°: highest pitch; 90°: steepest bank, slowest speed, pitch level; 135°: lowest pitch.
notes.explanation: Pitch peaks before bank does, so the nose traces a loop above and then below the horizon.

image.alt: A schematic of one 180-degree half of a lazy eight. A pitch curve rises above a level line, peaks, crosses level, dips below and returns to level. Points mark 0 degrees: level flight at entry airspeed; 45 degrees: maximum pitch up with about 15 degrees of bank; 90 degrees: pitch through level, maximum bank about 30 degrees, minimum airspeed 5 to 10 knots above stall; 135 degrees: lowest pitch attitude; 180 degrees: wings and nose level at the original airspeed.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10, "Lazy Eight" (see Figure 10-4)

notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: The reference points selected should be at 45°, 90°, and 135° from the direction in which the maneuver is started for each 180° turn.

notes.front: In a lazy eight, what should the airplane be doing as it reaches the 180° point?
notes.back: Wings and nose level at the original airspeed, then immediately start a climbing turn the other way.
notes.explanation: The second half repeats the first in the opposite direction, so there is no pause between them.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: Upon arriving at 180° point, a climbing turn should be started immediately in the opposite direction toward the preselected reference points to complete the second half of the lazy eight in the same manner as the first half.

notes.front: On the commercial test, what tolerances apply at the 180° point of a lazy eight?
notes.back: Altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots of the entry values, and heading ±10°.
notes.explanation: The manoeuvre is symmetrical, so each half should return to the entry altitude and airspeed.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task D "Lazy Eights", CA.V.D.S5
notes.evidence: Altitude at 180° point, ±100 feet from entry altitude CA.V.D.S5d d. Airspeed at the 180° point, ±10 knots from entry airspeed CA.V.D.S5e e. Heading at the 180° point, ±10°
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In a lazy eight, how do power and bank affect the altitude at the end of the manoeuvre?
notes.back: Too much power for the bank gains altitude; too little loses it.
notes.explanation: The handbook says power and bank angle have a significant effect on altitude; entry speed is generally no greater than VA.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: if excess power is used for a given bank angle, altitude is gained at the completion of the maneuver; however, if insufficient power is used for a given bank angle, altitude is lost.

notes.front: After each half of your lazy eights you are about 150 feet above the entry altitude, at the planned bank. What should you change?
notes.back: Reduce power.
notes.explanation: Gaining altitude at the planned bank means too much power, and 150 feet is outside the ±100-foot standard.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: Power and bank angle have significant effect on the altitude gained or lost; if excess power is used for a given bank angle, altitude is gained at the completion of the maneuver

notes.front: Between the 90° and 135° points of a lazy eight, how does right rudder pressure change, and why?
notes.back: It decreases, because airspeed increases as the pitch attitude decreases.
notes.explanation: Left-turning tendencies weaken as speed builds, so less right rudder keeps the ball centred.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: Pilots should remember that the airplane’s airspeed is increasing as the airplane’s pitch attitude decreases; therefore, maintaining proper coordination will require a decrease in right rudder pressure.

notes.front: Unlike turns around a point, does the turn around each pylon in eights on pylons need a constant radius and drift correction?
notes.back: No: there is no constant radius, so no drift correction is needed in the turn.
notes.explanation: The pilot holds a sight line on the pylon by changing altitude instead of holding a ground track.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: Since this maneuver does not require the turn to be completed at a constant radius, the pilot does not need to apply drift correction to complete the turn.

notes.front: What determines the pivotal altitude?
notes.back: The airplane's groundspeed.
notes.explanation: The rule of thumb for estimating it squares the groundspeed, so it changes as the heading changes relative to the wind.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: The altitude that is appropriate for eights on pylons is called the “pivotal altitude” and is determined by the airplane's groundspeed.

notes.front: To estimate pivotal altitude above the ground with groundspeed in knots, square the groundspeed and divide by {{c1::11.3}}.
notes.explanation: The result is then added to the ground reference's height above mean sea level.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: square the groundspeed, then divide by 15 (if the groundspeed is in miles per hour) or divide by 11.3 (if the groundspeed is in knots)

notes.front: To estimate pivotal altitude above the ground with groundspeed in miles per hour, square the groundspeed and divide by {{c1::15}}.
notes.explanation: The divisor is larger than for knots because a speed in miles per hour is a bigger number.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: square the groundspeed, then divide by 15 (if the groundspeed is in miles per hour) or divide by 11.3 (if the groundspeed is in knots)

notes.front: After squaring the groundspeed and dividing, what must be added to get the pivotal altitude on the altimeter?
notes.back: The ground reference's elevation above mean sea level.
notes.explanation: The rule of thumb gives height above the pylon, and the altimeter reads height above sea level.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: and then add the mean sea level (MSL) altitude of the ground reference.

notes.front: Your groundspeed is 100 knots and the pylons stand on ground 800 feet above sea level. Roughly what pivotal altitude do you set?
notes.back: About 1,685 feet above sea level (10,000 ÷ 11.3 ≈ 885, plus 800).
notes.explanation: Square the groundspeed in knots, divide by 11.3, then add the ground elevation.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: square the groundspeed, then divide by 15 (if the groundspeed is in miles per hour) or divide by 11.3 (if the groundspeed is in knots), and then add the mean sea level (MSL) altitude of the ground reference.

notes.front: Your groundspeed is 120 miles per hour and the pylons are on ground 500 feet above sea level. Roughly what pivotal altitude do you set?
notes.back: About 1,460 feet above sea level (14,400 ÷ 15 = 960, plus 500).
notes.explanation: With miles per hour the divisor is 15; the ground elevation is then added.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: square the groundspeed, then divide by 15 (if the groundspeed is in miles per hour) or divide by 11.3 (if the groundspeed is in knots), and then add the mean sea level (MSL) altitude of the ground reference.

notes.front: Does the bank angle chosen for eights on pylons change the pivotal altitude?
notes.back: No, unless the bank is steep enough to affect the groundspeed.
notes.explanation: Pivotal altitude depends on groundspeed, and bank only sets how far from the pylon the airplane turns.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: The pivotal altitude does not vary with the angle of bank unless the bank is steep enough to affect the groundspeed.

notes.front: Your instructor has you enter closer to the pylon, so the steepest bank rises from 25° to 35°. The wind and groundspeed are unchanged. Do you fly higher, lower or at the same altitude?
notes.back: At the same pivotal altitude.
notes.explanation: Moving closer changes the bank, but the bank chosen does not alter the pivotal altitude.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: The pilot should understand that the bank chosen does not alter the pivotal altitude.

notes.front: As the airplane turns to head upwind around a pylon, what happens to the pivotal altitude, and what does the pilot do?
notes.back: Groundspeed falls, which lowers the pivotal altitude, so the pilot descends.
notes.explanation: Descending keeps the visual reference line on the pylon as the groundspeed changes.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: As the airplane heads upwind, the groundspeed decreases, which lowers the pivotal altitude. As a result, the pilot should descend to hold the visual reference line on the pylon.

notes.front: Around a pylon you turn from an upwind heading toward a downwind one. Should you expect to climb or descend to hold the pylon?
notes.back: Climb: the higher groundspeed raises the pivotal altitude.
notes.explanation: Pivotal altitude changes with groundspeed, and groundspeed rises as the heading turns downwind.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: The pivotal altitude changes with variations in groundspeed. Since the headings throughout turns continuously vary from downwind to upwind, the groundspeed constantly changes.

notes.front: When the airplane is above the pivotal altitude, which way does the projected reference line appear to move relative to the pylon?
notes.back: Rearward (backward); below the pivotal altitude it appears to move forward.
notes.explanation: The line only stays still at the pivotal altitude, which is how the pilot finds it.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: At any altitude above that pivotal altitude, the projected reference line appears to move rearward in a circular path in relation to the pylon. Conversely, when the airplane is below the pivotal altitude, the projected reference line appears to move forward in a circular path.

notes.front: In eights on pylons, the reference line moves ahead of the pylon (the pylon appears to move back). What does the pilot do?
notes.back: Increase altitude.
notes.explanation: A line moving forward means the airplane is below the pivotal altitude.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: If the visual reference line appears to move ahead of the pylon (pylon appears to move back), the pilot should increase altitude.

notes.front: In eights on pylons, the reference line moves behind the pylon (the pylon appears to move ahead). What does the pilot do?
notes.back: Decrease altitude.
notes.explanation: A line moving backward means the airplane is above the pivotal altitude.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: If the visual reference line appears to move behind the pylon (pylon appears to move ahead), the pilot should decrease altitude.

notes.front: Turning around a pylon, you see it slide back behind your reference line. Your student pushes inside rudder to yaw the wing back onto it. What should they do instead?
notes.back: Climb, keeping the rudder for coordination only.
notes.explanation: The pylon moving back means the airplane is below the pivotal altitude; yawing with rudder puts it in uncoordinated flight at low altitude and steep bank.
notes.choices:
A) Hold the inside rudder until the pylon returns
B) Climb, using rudder only for coordination
C) Descend, using rudder only for coordination
D) Steepen the bank with outside rudder
notes.choicesExplained: A is the most common error the handbook names: yawing with rudder. C is the correction for a pylon that moves ahead. D mixes a bank change with an uncoordinated rudder input.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: Deflecting the rudder to yaw the airplane and force the wing and reference line forward or backward to the pylon places the airplane in uncoordinated flight, at low altitude, with steep bank angles and should not be attempted.

notes.front: What is the most common error when trying to hold a pylon?
notes.back: Incorrect use of the rudder: yawing the wing toward the pylon instead of using rudder only for coordination.
notes.explanation: The pylon is held by altitude changes, not by skidding or slipping the airplane.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons", common errors
notes.evidence: The most common error in attempting to hold a pylon is incorrect use of the rudder.

notes.front: Should the pilot correct pivotal altitude by watching the altimeter?
notes.back: No: that is ineffective; corrections follow the apparent movement of the reference line.
notes.explanation: Pylon position varies with the sight line, and pivotal altitude varies through the turn with groundspeed.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: It is important to understand that variations in pylon position are according to the apparent movement of the visual reference line. Attempting to correct pivotal altitude by the using the altimeter is ineffective.

notes.front: How should eights on pylons be entered?
notes.back: Diagonally crosswind between the pylons to a point downwind of the first, so the first turn is into the wind.
notes.explanation: Not entering the pylon turns into the wind is listed as a common error.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 7 "Ground Reference Maneuvers", "Eights on Pylons"
notes.evidence: The pilot should begin the eight on pylons maneuver by flying diagonally crosswind between the pylons to a point downwind from the first pylon, so that the first turn can be made into the wind.

notes.front: On the commercial test, what is the bank limit for eights on pylons?
notes.back: Not to exceed 40°.
notes.explanation: The bank is chosen for the conditions, within this cap, while holding the pylon at the pivotal altitude.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task E "Eights on Pylons", CA.V.E.S5
notes.evidence: Establish the correct bank angle for the conditions, not to exceed 40°.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What is the real basis of all power-off accuracy approaches and landings?
notes.back: The ability to estimate the distance the airplane glides to a landing.
notes.explanation: The distance to cover largely decides how much manoeuvring the approach needs from a given height.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "Power-Off Accuracy Approaches"
notes.evidence: The ability to estimate the distance an airplane glides to a landing is the real basis of all power-off accuracy approaches and landings.

notes.front: Why does the commercial test include a power-off 180° accuracy landing, when normal landings use power?
notes.back: To build judgement of glide distance and planning so the airplane can be flown to a safe landing without power.
notes.explanation: The handbook states this objective, and the task asks the applicant to explain the purpose of the approach.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "Power-Off Accuracy Approaches"
notes.evidence: The objective is to instill in the pilot the judgment and procedures necessary for accurately flying the airplane, without power, to a safe landing.

notes.front: On a power-off approach, what controls airspeed?
notes.back: Pitch attitude, because power is fixed at idle.
notes.explanation: Changing pitch also changes the glide angle, so speed and path are managed together.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "Power-Off Accuracy Approaches"
notes.evidence: Unlike a normal approach when the power setting is variable, on a power-off approach the power is fixed at the idle setting. Pitch attitude is adjusted to control the airspeed.

notes.front: Gliding faster than best glide speed, you are a little low. What does raising the nose toward best glide do to the descent angle?
notes.back: It shallows the descent angle while reducing airspeed.
notes.explanation: Above best glide speed, pitching up reduces airspeed and shallows the descent.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "Power-Off Accuracy Approaches"
notes.evidence: If an airplane is on approach with an airspeed higher than best glide, pitching down will increase the airspeed and steepen the descent angle, while pitching up will reduce the airspeed and shallow the descent angle.

notes.front: Gliding below best glide speed and short of the spot, a pilot raises the nose to stretch the glide. What happens?
notes.back: Airspeed falls and the descent angle steepens greatly: the airplane lands shorter.
notes.explanation: Below best glide, pitching up greatly steepens the descent, which is why a glide should never be stretched.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "Power-Off Accuracy Approaches"
notes.evidence: Conversely, if the airspeed is below best glide, then pitching down will increase the airspeed and shallow the descent angle, while pitching up will reduce the airspeed and will greatly steepen the descent angle.

notes.front: Why should a pilot never try to stretch a glide to reach the landing spot?
notes.back: With the pitch too high, the airplane settles rapidly from slow airspeed and insufficient lift.
notes.explanation: Stretching the glide during an undershoot is listed among the common errors of these approaches.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "Power-Off Accuracy Approaches"
notes.evidence: If the pitch attitude is raised too high, the airplane settles rapidly due to a slow airspeed and insufficient lift. For this reason, the pilot should never try to stretch a glide to reach the desired landing spot.

notes.front: Should a pilot sacrifice a good approach or landing to touch down on the chosen spot?
notes.back: No: a good landing away from the spot is better than a poor one on it.
notes.explanation: Accurate touchdowns matter, but safe, properly flown approaches and landings are vital.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "90° Power-Off Approach"
notes.evidence: It is always better to execute a good landing away from the spot than to make a poor landing precisely on or just past the spot.

notes.front: On short final in a power-off 180 you see you will float about 300 feet past the spot. What should you do?
notes.back: Make a good, safe landing past the spot rather than force the airplane onto it.
notes.explanation: Forcing the airplane on to avoid overshooting is a listed common error, and a good landing away from the spot is preferred.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "Power-Off Accuracy Approaches", common errors
notes.evidence: Forcing the airplane onto the runway in order to avoid overshooting the designated landing spot.

notes.front: In the 180-degree power-off approach, when is the throttle closed?
notes.back: When abreast of (opposite) the landing spot on downwind; that point is the downwind key position.
notes.explanation: Altitude is then held while the airplane slows to the recommended glide speed or 1.4 VS0.

image.alt: A plan view of a runway with a selected landing spot. The downwind leg runs parallel to the runway in the opposite direction. A red dot abeam the spot marks the downwind key position where the throttle is closed. The glide path curves through a turn past the base key position, which is not a fixed landmark, and onto final to the spot. A shaded box shows touchdown on the spot or within 200 feet beyond it.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9, "180° Power-Off Approach" (see Figure 9-27), and the Commercial Pilot ACS, Task IV.M

notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "180° Power-Off Approach"
notes.evidence: When abreast of or opposite the desired landing spot, the throttle is closed and altitude maintained while decelerating to the manufacturer’s recommended glide speed or 1.4 VSO. The point at which the throttle is closed is the downwind key position.
uses: stalling speed in the landing configuration

notes.front: After closing the throttle abeam the spot, what speed does the pilot decelerate to if there is no manufacturer's glide speed?
notes.explanation: Altitude is held while slowing, so the glide begins from a known speed and height each time.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "180° Power-Off Approach"
notes.evidence: the throttle is closed and altitude maintained while decelerating to the manufacturer’s recommended glide speed or 1.4 VSO.
uses: stalling speed in the landing configuration

notes.front: On the commercial test, the power-off 180° landing must touch down {{c1::on or within 200 feet beyond}} the specified point.
notes.explanation: The allowance is only beyond the point, so any touchdown short of it does not meet the standard.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation IV, Task M "Power-Off 180° Accuracy Approach and Landing", CA.IV.M.S8
notes.evidence: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude, within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point with no side drift
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: On a commercial checkride your power-off 180 touches down 40 feet before the specified point. Does it meet the standard?
notes.back: No: the touchdown must be on the point or up to 200 feet beyond it.
notes.explanation: The tolerance runs only past the point, so even a small undershoot is outside it.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it is within ±200 feet
B) No, landing short of the point is outside the standard
C) Yes, if the touchdown was smooth
D) Yes, anything within 100 feet either side passes
notes.choicesExplained: A treats the tolerance as plus or minus, but it runs only beyond the point. C: a smooth touchdown does not change the distance standard. D invents a tolerance the standard does not give.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation IV, Task M "Power-Off 180° Accuracy Approach and Landing", CA.IV.M.S8
notes.evidence: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude, within 200 feet beyond or on the specified point with no side drift
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: In a 180-degree power-off approach, how is the base leg used to manage the glide?
notes.back: It is positioned as needed to conserve or dissipate altitude to reach the spot.
notes.explanation: The downwind-to-base turn and base position depend on the glide angle and the wind.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "180° Power-Off Approach"
notes.evidence: Again, the base leg is positioned as needed for the altitude or wind condition. Position the base leg to conserve or dissipate altitude so as to reach the desired landing spot.

notes.front: During a power-off accuracy approach, what throttle use is a common error?
notes.back: Using the throttle to increase the glide instead of merely clearing the engine.
notes.explanation: Power is fixed at idle, so adding it to extend the glide defeats the exercise.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 9 "Approaches and Landings", "Power-Off Accuracy Approaches", common errors
notes.evidence: Use of throttle to increase the glide instead of merely clearing the engine.

notes.front: On the commercial power-off 180 task, how is a forward slip used in a crosswind?
notes.back: The slip direction is matched to the crosswind, transitioning to a sideslip before touchdown.
notes.explanation: The touchdown must have no side drift, with the longitudinal axis over the centreline.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation IV, Task M "Power-Off 180° Accuracy Approach and Landing", CA.IV.M.S7
notes.evidence: As necessary, correlate crosswind with direction of forward slip and transition to side slip before touchdown.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What bank does the private steep-turn task ask for, compared with the commercial one?
notes.back: Private: approximately 45°. Commercial: approximately 50°.
notes.explanation: The tolerances are the same on both tests; only the target bank differs.
notes.source: Private Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-6C), Area of Operation V, Task A "Steep Turns", PA.V.A.S3 and S5
notes.evidence: Roll into a coordinated 360° steep turn with approximately a 45° bank. PA.V.A.S4 Perform the Task in the opposite direction, as specified by evaluator. PA.V.A.S5 Maintain the entry altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, bank ±5°, and roll out on the entry heading ±10°.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: How do control inputs in a chandelle differ from those in a lazy eight?
notes.back: The chandelle holds bank, then pitch, constant; in the lazy eight control pressures change all the time.
notes.explanation: Both are 180° climbing turns, but only the lazy eight descends again and never holds a steady input.
notes.source: Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), chapter 10 "Performance Maneuvers", "Lazy Eight"
notes.evidence: It is the only standard flight training maneuver in which flight control pressures are constantly changing.

notes.front: Which commercial manoeuvre has a bank limit of "not to exceed 60°" at the steepest point?
notes.back: The steep spiral.
notes.explanation: The spiral bank is steepest on downwind headings, and this cap applies there.
notes.choices:
A) Eights on pylons
B) Lazy eight
C) Steep turn
D) Steep spiral
notes.choicesExplained: A is capped at 40°. B uses about 30° at the steepest point. C targets about 50°, ±5°.
notes.source: Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category ACS (FAA-S-ACS-7B), Area of Operation V, Task B "Steep Spiral", CA.V.B.S3
notes.evidence: Establish and maintain a steep spiral, not to exceed 60° angle of bank, to maintain a constant radius about a suitable ground reference point.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-7B and 14 CFR as in force
